8aa11e1fa3954e26: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 1 — On the grasslands of Xinjiang, horses are more than animals used for transport.
For generations, they have been part of everyday life, carrying traditions, memories and a close connection between families and the land they call home.
This relationship between people and horses forms the backdrop of The Little Horsewhip, a coming-of-age film that follows young Angsar and the bond he develops with his horse, Flyk.
Beyond Angsar’s story, the film also showcases Xinjiang’s landscapes and Kazakh customs, while exploring themes of rural life and the preservation and passing down of cultural traditions.
Directed by Xinwen Dong and Xiapukati Mulati, the film made its Malaysian cinema debut today, three years after its release in China in 2023.

The film previously received recognition, including the Outstanding Children’s Film Award at the 20th China Huabiao Film Awards and the Best Film Award at the 28th International Children’s and Youth Film Festival.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
‘The Little Horsewhip’ producer Li XiaoBing (centre-right) with members of the team behind the film at its press screening at Pavilion Bukit Jalil. — Picture courtesy of Click Entertainment
A cultural bridge between Xinjiang and Malaysia

Speaking to Malay Mail, producer Li Xiaobing, who is also director of the Theory Division of the Publicity Department of the Party Committee of the Autonomous Region, said it was meaningful for the film to reach Malaysian audiences.
“The film is like a sincere invitation from Xinjiang, and we hope this screening can serve as a small cultural bridge,” he said.

Set against the Xinjiang grasslands, the film follows Angsar as he grows up surrounded by family and friends, while learning about patience, responsibility and trust through his relationship with Flyk.
Li said the story also offered an opportunity to introduce audiences outside China to the region’s landscapes and cultural traditions through a child’s experiences.

“Although Xinjiang and Malaysia are far apart, we hope Malaysian audiences can see the beautiful grasslands of Xinjiang and experience the genuine warmth of ordinary people’s lives through this child’s story of growing up.
“To see our story cross borders and form an emotional connection with audiences from different cultural backgrounds is something we truly cherish,” he said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The press screening of ‘The Little Horsewhip’ at Pavilion Bukit Jalil on September 29, 2026. — Picture courtesy of Click Entertainment
The inspiration behind The Little Horsewhip
The film’s depiction of horse culture drew inspiration from the real-life “Equestrianism in Schools” programme implemented in Altay, Xinjiang.
The creative team travelled to local grasslands and horse ranches, where they conducted field visits and spoke to local herders.
They observed children learning to ride horses, taking part in equestrian competitions and caring for their animals — experiences that later informed the film.

“The complete story of Angsar is fictional, but many of the details of grassland life and equestrian traditions portrayed in the film are based on the real-life experiences and observations we encountered firsthand,” Li said.

Traditional clothing, yurts, saddles, horsewhips and carved wooden bowls are also incorporated into the story, while grasslands, forests, rivers and snow-covered mountains provide the backdrop to Angsar’s journey.
Li said the creative team had considered how a story rooted in Xinjiang could connect with audiences from other countries.
While the film carries strong regional characteristics, he said its central emotions were universal.
“The film follows a child as he grows up with the companionship of family and friends, while pursuing his dreams and learning about patience, responsibility and trust,” he said.
Li said audiences from different backgrounds could relate to Angsar’s aspirations, his relationship with Flyk and the challenges he faces while growing up.
“We hope international audiences can see a more complete and vivid picture of Xinjiang.

“At the same time, themes such as children pursuing their dreams, people and animals accompanying and supporting one another, and having respect for nature are emotions that can resonate with people around the world,” he said.
Capturing Xinjiang through all four seasons

Much of The Little Horsewhip was filmed on location in Xinjiang across all four seasons, capturing the changing landscapes of the Altai region, from green grasslands and forests to rivers, villages and snow-covered terrain.
Filming also came with challenges, particularly when working with horses and children amid rapidly changing weather conditions.
The production team had to adapt to the animals’ behaviour and wait for suitable weather rather than expecting nature to follow the filming schedule.
Li said this approach helped the film retain a more natural atmosphere.
He also hoped audiences would look beyond the scenery and understand the relationship between people and horses that remains part of life on the grasslands.
“I hope audiences can understand the kindness, courage and respect for life found among the people of the grasslands, and experience the deep and unique bond between people and horses.
“More than simply remembering the magnificent scenery of Xinjiang, we hope audiences can also feel the simplicity, sincerity and warmth of human relationships on the grasslands,” he said.
At its centre, however, The Little Horsewhip remains a story about a child, a horse and the experiences that shape him as he grows up.
For Angsar, the grasslands become the place where he learns about dreams, friendship and responsibility — with Flyk beside him along the way.
The Little Horsewhip opened in Malaysian cinemas nationwide today.
19b9e4cabac9b9e9: SINGAPORE: The dollar touched a more than three-month high on Thursday, supported by an extended rise in US Treasury yields that has been partly driven by concerns about persistent global price pressures stemming from the US-Israeli war on Iran.

Data showing US inflation rose less than expected in August, along with downward revisions to July's reading, reduced expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike this month. But a surge in euro zone inflation underscored the threat that higher energy prices continue to pose to the global economy.
Against the dollar, the euro fell 0.11% to US$1.1317 in Asia. It clocked a loss of nearly 2.5% in September, the largest since July 2025, pressured by Europe's debt and energy worries.

Sterling edged 0.1% lower to US$1.32495 after having slid 2.1% last month, similarly weighed down by a stronger greenback. The dollar peaked at 101.66 against a basket of currencies, its highest level since June 25, extending its 2% rise in September.

"The US dollar seems to be showing more sensitivity, just at the moment, to what's happening with say, 10-year Treasuries, than it is on pricing for when the next Fed rate hike might come," said Ray Attrill, head of FX strategy at National Australia Bank.

"While yields are continuing to rise for the time being, I think it's supportive for the dollar. If we do get an inflection point where it starts to really hurt the equity market, the dollar can benefit from that."
Global bonds suffered their largest monthly decline in years in September, pushing yields higher, due to a toxic mix of deteriorating government finances, a glut of issuances and rising inflation.

The scaling back of expectations for a Fed hike this month prompted a slight retreat in shorter-dated US Treasury yields, but 10- and 30-year yields still hit new highs in the previous session. They hovered near those levels on Thursday.
Against the yen, the dollar was up 0.54% at 158.29 after falling 1.4% against the Japanese currency last month.

"The yen has been the strongest of the G10 currencies (in September), and the market's reluctance to be caught out by intervention is clearly having an impact," said Kit Juckes, chief FX strategist at Societe Generale.

Some Bank of Japan policymakers saw the need to accelerate the pace of interest rate hikes or bring them closer to the central bank's "goal" soon, a summary of opinions at its September meeting showed on Thursday.

The Australian dollar fell to a two-month low of US$0.6940 on Thursday, as investors lengthened the odds on another near-term rate hike from the Reserve Bank of Australia after domestic inflation came in slightly lower than forecast.
The New Zealand dollar similarly slid to its lowest point since November 2025 at US$0.5618.
3427487700555f19: PUTRAJAYA: Bekas perdana menteri, Dr Mahathir Mohamad menziarahi pusara Dr Hasmah Mohd Ali di Pusara Negara pada 11.05 pagi tadi, empat hari selepas pemergian isterinya.

Terdahulu, anak sulung pasangan itu, Marina Mahathir hadir menziarahi pusara ibunya pada kira-kira 10 pagi.
Sementara itu, antara yang turut menziarahi ialah bekas jaguh badminton negara, Lee Chong Wei, penyanyi Ramli Sarip dan Ahli Parlimen Putrajaya Radzi Jidin.

Berkongsi dengan media, Lee berkata antara kenangan yang tidak dapat dilupakannya adalah sikap Hasmah yang sentiasa menghubungi atlet untuk bertanya khabar, terutama selepas mereka menyertai sesuatu kejohanan.
“Apabila beliau datang berjumpa kami di stadium, beliau akan tanya seorang demi seorang. ‘How are you? Beliau ingat keperluan setiap atlet.
“Beliau sentiasa mengambil berat tentang kami. Itu yang kami (rasa) kehilangan, seorang tokoh yang begitu dekat dengan badminton,” katanya.
Lee berkata Hasmah turut memberikan kata-kata semangat ketika atlet berdepan kekalahan di samping terus menyokong mereka tanpa mengira keputusan yang dicapai.
“Ketika kami menang, beliau akan hantar mesej kepada kami..apabila kami kalah, ketika itulah kami lebih memerlukan sokongan dan beliau tidak pernah berputus asa dengan kami.

“Beliau akan telefon atau hantar mesej dan berkata, ‘It’s okay, you try your best, you have played very well’. Jangan berputus asa, teruskan usaha. Itu yang saya tidak akan lupakan sepanjang karier saya sebagai atlet,” katanya.
Katanya, beliau menerima berita pemergian Hasmah ketika berada di Nagoya, Jepun selepas selesai menyertai kejohanan di Filipina.
“Saya rasa seluruh pasukan badminton turut bersedih dengan berita itu. Kami hanya mampu mendoakan beliau,” katanya.
Beliau berkata sebaik tiba di Malaysia, beliau bersama isteri yang juga bekas pemain badminton negara, Wong Mew Choo terus menziarahi pusara Hasmah sebagai tanda penghormatan terakhir.

63b643faa9697186: PETALING JAYA: Suruhanjaya Pencegahan Rasuah Malaysia (SPRM) menegaskan pihaknya tidak menyerahkan notis pengisytiharan harta kepada anak lelaki bekas menteri sumber manusia M Saravanan yang berusia 12 tahun.

21cf8c0475c5ed2f: BANGKOK: Bangkok’s severe flooding is hitting Thailand’s fragile economy where it’s most vulnerable, wiping out incomes for small businesses and workers already burdened by high debt and stretching the government’s finances.

The disruption has been immediate for thousands of street vendors, drivers and other informal workers who don’t get paid if they can’t get to work. Nearly a week of flooding has brought parts of the capital’s informal economy to a standstill, even as initial estimates suggest only a modest hit to national growth.

That matters because Bangkok and its surrounding provinces generate roughly half of Thailand’s economic output. Thai Airways International Pcl cut flights and suspended cargo intake, while automakers including Honda Motor and Toyota Motor halted some production.

For smaller businesses and workers paid by the day, the losses can be harder to absorb. Restaurants in flood-hit areas have reported losing as much as 80% of their revenue, as customers, employees and delivery drivers struggle to reach them.

“My income has fallen to zero,” said Somchai Onsarn, a street vendor who typically makes about 3,000 baht (US$89) a day selling cosmetics. The area where he usually sets up his stall remains flooded. “I couldn’t go out to sell anything.”

Initial estimates paint a less severe picture at the national level. The University of the Thai Chamber of Commerce estimates flooding in Bangkok and dozens of provinces could shave about 0.07 percentage point off economic growth, equivalent to as much as 12.3 billion baht in losses. The damage could double if flooding persists and disrupts more activity.

“The estimates may not yet capture the full extent of the damage,” said Tim Leelahaphan, a Bangkok-based economist at Standard Chartered Plc. “They can also mask the impact on more vulnerable groups, with low-income households likely to be hit hardest.”

Kae, a tuk-tuk driver, said being trapped at home meant losing the fares he depends on for his livelihood. “When I couldn’t leave my home, I couldn’t earn anything,” he said. “The economic impact feels very different on the ground from what the estimates suggest.”

The floods are hitting an economy with little cushion. Thailand is expected to grow only about 2%-2.5% this year. It also has one of Asia’s highest levels of household debt, which constrains consumption and leaves many families with limited capacity to withstand even a temporary loss of earnings.

“Small businesses and vulnerable groups could face a heavier debt burden,” said Chayawadee Chai-anant, an assistant governor at the Bank of Thailand. “Successive economic shocks are weakening their balance sheets. That is quite worrying.”

Prime minister Anutin Charnvirakul’s government has approved about 4 billion baht (US$119 million) in immediate flood relief, but it has its own borrowing constraints. The budget deficit is running at about 4% of GDP, and public debt was already forecast to climb very close to the self-imposed ceiling of 70%, limiting room for large relief programmes.

Climate change threatens to make demands for such efforts more frequent. Thailand doesn’t include climate in its annual fiscal-risk reports, according to Athiphat Muthitacharoen, a budget policy specialist.

More frequent floods, droughts and other extreme weather could require greater spending on relief and reconstruction even as an aging population puts increasing pressure on health and welfare budgets.

a78504c580bd6c6a: FRANKFURT: European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde has raised the possibility of leaving her post early, telling Wednesday's edition of French newspaper La Croix she could not rule out stepping down a few months before her term expires.

"I do not exclude the possibility of stepping down a few months before the end of my term, but I have not announced anything concrete, and one thing is certain: In 2027 I will still be here," Lagarde said, reported German news agency dpa.
"So if I do step down early, it will only be a matter of a few months. It will not turn the world upside down," said the Frenchwoman, whose eight-year term runs until October 2027.

Lagarde ruled out standing in France's presidential election in April 2027. "That would not be a good idea at all," she said when asked. It was not a comparable job, she said. "On the one hand, it requires vitality, energy and strength. On the other hand, such a commitment inevitably involves certain sacrifices. And I am 70 years old."
Asked whether she wanted to take part in debates ahead of the 2027 French presidential election, Lagarde said vaguely: "My task now is to serve the European public interest."

Speculation about Lagarde's future has been circulating for months. She has been linked to the World Economic Forum in Davos, and there have been reports that she wants to step down before the French presidential election in April and May. The backdrop is concern that right-wing populists could win the election, which could complicate the appointment of a new ECB chief.

Lagarde had previously reaffirmed that she would not leave before 2027. "When clouds appear on the horizon, the captain stays on the ship. And there are clouds on the horizon," she said in July. Before that, she had not ruled out an early departure from her post, citing the French presidential election.

1fafbd910093b204: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 1 — Disaster management is challenging, but the National Disaster Management Agency’s (Nadma) commitment to preparedness remains key to supporting people when the country faces disasters, said Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi.

8edc8cb85f7707a9: PETALING JAYA: An Indonesian man was sentenced to 13 years’ jail by the Tawau High Court today after pleading guilty to causing the death of a compatriot who raped his 12-year-old daughter.

According to the facts of the case, the incident occurred after the accused’s daughter told her mother that she had been raped on the way home from an event.
Upon hearing this, the accused grabbed a parang and chased the man, cornering him near a chicken coop before slashing him several times.

A medical examination found tears in the daughter’s genital area, while a chemistry department analysis found that the deceased’s DNA was on her nails and matched DNA from semen found on her underwear.

f9ba23590baf080f: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 1 — An Indonesian father of six has been sentenced to 13 years in prison for causing the death of a compatriot after his 12-year-old daughter said the man had raped her, with subsequent forensic tests linking the victim to the alleged assault.
The 30-year-old pleaded guilty at the High Court in Tawau to an alternative charge over the death of the 33-year-old man in August 2024, the New Straits Times (NST) reported.
He had initially been charged with murder under Section 302 of the Penal Code, but the charge was later amended to one under Section 304(a), which covers culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
Judicial Commissioner Steve Ritikos ordered the 13-year prison term to run from September 2, 2024, the date of the accused’s arrest.
The court also ordered that he be referred to the Immigration Department after completing his sentence.

According to the facts of the case, the incident began after the accused’s daughter, who was 12 at the time, told her mother that the victim had raped her while she was returning from a social gathering on the night of August 31, 2024.
After learning of the allegation, the accused armed himself with a parang and went looking for the man.
He later chased the victim to a nearby chicken coop and slashed him several times.
The victim died sometime between 7.30pm on August 31 and noon the following day at an unnumbered house in Tawau.
Forensic analysis by the Chemistry Department Malaysia found the victim’s DNA on clippings taken from the girl’s fingernails.
The DNA profile from semen found on her underwear also matched that of the victim, according to the facts presented in court.
Police arrested the accused at his home on September 2, 2024, and seized the parang used in the attack.
An offence under Section 304(a) of the Penal Code carries a maximum prison sentence of 30 years and a fine.
Deputy public prosecutor Nur Nisla Abd Latif appeared for the prosecution, while lawyer Jhessery P. Kang represented the accused.

5a3d5ff447508845: The grief that swept across Malaysia following the passing of Dr Hasmah Ali, wife of former prime minister Dr Mahathir Mohamad, was nothing short of extraordinary.
It was a heartfelt farewell befitting the nation’s most beloved First Lady — a woman whose unwavering presence beside her husband was a story of devotion in itself.

And the tributes have not stopped. From Malaysians of every race, every creed, every walk of life, the outpouring has been relentless — a rare sight that has moved many to tears. Even days after her final bow, the love remains.
But it was a scene in Hasmah’s final send-off that will forever be etched in the hearts of Malaysians yearning for unity. A scene that spoke louder than any policy or speech.
There was Mahathir, at 101 years old, in his wheelchair, tears streaming down his face as he bade farewell to his partner of a lifetime.

And standing behind him, in a silent show of solidarity, were three individuals: a Malay doctor, an Indian nurse, and a Chinese physiotherapist. The physiotherapist, himself fighting back tears, gently held tissues to wipe away the former PM’s tears, ensuring he was okay.
It was a fleeting moment, but it said everything.

This was the dream. This was the “Bangsa Malaysia” that Mahathir envisioned when he launched Vision 2020 back in 1991. Sadly, it never fully materialised even though he returned for a second stint in office in 2018.
But here, inadvertently and coincidentally, at the most vulnerable moment of his life, the nation watched it unfold “live”.
It was a powerful reminder that Malaysia cannot survive, cannot thrive, without all its citizens — each playing their part, especially when times are tough.

This was how the older generations lived. This was how they built the nation. Race and religion were afterthoughts; what mattered was the Malaysian standing before them, bringing glory to the nation, regardless of skin colour.
And then there were the pictures.

Two photographs posted by badminton legend Lee Chong Wei in his tear-jerking tribute to Hasmah — whom he lovingly called a motherly figure to him and his wife. As patron of the Badminton Association of Malaysia during Chong Wei’s glorious reign, she was more than a figurehead; she was family.

In the first photo, Chong Wei is seen walking forward, hand outstretched in greeting. But what happened next took everyone’s breath away. Hasmah, instead of a formal handshake, opened her arms wide and pulled him into a warm, enveloping hug.
It was a simple gesture. But in that embrace, she showed Malaysians something profound: that despite our different colours and creeds, we are, and always will be, one race. The human race.
There is so much for Malaysian politicians to learn from this episode.
There were more instances that showed the Malaysian in Hasmah but you need to write a book to document everything.
Rest in peace, Hasmah. You taught us how to live, how to love, and in your passing, how to unite.

11b9d330370e3dd5: There was something slightly strange about watching Malaysian athletics in Nagoya.
Some of the loudest Malaysian cheers belonged to two sprinters wearing Thai and Singaporean colours.
Puripol Boonson came tearing down the home straight and it was impossible not to watch. Shanti Pereira emerged from the bend in the rain and Malaysians could only marvel.
Perhaps that is what sport is supposed to do. Excellence has no passport.
But it also leaves Malaysian athletics with an uncomfortable question.
What happens when a country’s supporters begin looking across the border for something to believe in?
Boonson gave them plenty.

The 20-year-old Thai won the 100m in 9.90 seconds, a Games record, then produced an astonishing 19.88 in the 200m to complete the sprint double. His 200m time matched China’s Xie Zhenye’s Asian record.
His race had a particular drama. The start was not spectacular. Then he began to eat up the bend before powering into the straight, opening daylight between himself and the field.
Pereira provided a different kind of spectacle.

On a rain-swept track, the Singaporean defended her 200m title in 22.78 seconds. She did not have the fastest start, but built her race around the curve before producing the strongest finish. She became the first woman to win the Asian Games 200m twice.
These were not simply victories. They looked like performances built on purpose.
That is where the comparison with Malaysia becomes uncomfortable.
Malaysia sent 20 athletes to the athletics programme. Only Azeem Fahmi and Danish Iftikhar Roslee reached individual finals, in the 100m and 200m respectively.
Azeem's race ended painfully when muscle cramps forced him to slow almost to a walk before he crossed in 14.65 seconds. Danish finished sixth in 20.89.
There were young athletes who gained experience and made progress. That should be acknowledged. But too many performances offered little evidence of where the next breakthrough might come from.
And this was not an isolated bad week.
The last two years have brought coaching disputes, questions over athlete development and competition, organisational controversies and a growing sense of drift.
There have been changes and new structures, but Nagoya should force a more prickly question: have those changes actually improved the system?
There are no quick fixes for an illness. But before treatment can begin, someone has to admit the patient is sick.
The worrying thing about Malaysian athletics is not simply that it has come home without a medal. It is whether there is enough urgency to suggest that the result has forced a reckoning.
If Malaysia Athletics thinks Nagoya was an aberration, it risks adding another problem to the list: self-delusion.

Athletics is brutally competitive. Malaysia is not simply competing against its Southeast Asian neighbours. Seventeen countries had won athletics medals in Nagoya, while Malaysia remained outside the medal table.
That should temper the argument, not weaken it.
The question is not why Malaysia did not beat China, Japan or India.
It is why neighbouring countries are producing athletes capable of making Asia sit up and watch.
Look at Boonson.
His development stretches back through school athletics and national structures, with coaching support that has continued to evolve as he has moved towards the senior level.
Look at Pereira.

Her progress has been built over years with coach Luis Cunha, who has worked on the smallest details of her sprinting, from mechanics to acceleration and the ability to squeeze more from an already accomplished athlete.
That is the comparison worth making.
Not whether Thailand or Singapore has discovered a secret formula. But whether Malaysia has built an environment in which talented athletes can keep getting better.
Danish, 19, offers a revealing case.

At last year’s SEA Games, he finished third in the 100m and 200m behind Boonson. He has since emerged as one of Malaysia's most promising young sprinters, holding the national 200m record of 20.73 seconds.
That is progress, but Boonson was progressing too. What is Thailand doing to keep moving its young sprinter forward? That is a system question, not an indictment of Danish.
The same distinction must apply across the Malaysian team. Athletes are responsible for their training, discipline, recovery and performance.

They cannot build the national development system around them, recruit specialist coaches, create an international competition programme, resolve disputes between associations or determine how promising juniors are identified and moved into the senior ranks.
This is where Malaysia Athletics needs to be honest. Where is the pathway from junior to senior athletics? How many athletes who emerge at Sukma become international contenders?

How are coaches evaluated and what happens when an athlete stagnates? What level of sports-science support is available, and how much meaningful international competition do promising athletes receive?
Most importantly, who is accountable when the system does not deliver?
There are encouraging signs. Nine Sukma records were broken at the 2026 Games, suggesting Malaysia still has young athletes capable of progress.
But what happens to that progression once they move from promising youngster to senior international athlete?

Malaysia Athletics should consider an independent examination of its high-performance system covering coaching, talent identification, junior development, state associations, competition planning, sports science, athlete welfare, selection and funding.
This should not become a hunt for convenient scapegoats. It should begin with a more basic question: what did Malaysia Athletics promise, and what did it actually deliver?
The answer matters because Kuala Lumpur hosts the SEA Games next year.
Home advantage can produce medals. It cannot manufacture a high-performance system.
A successful SEA Games could even make the problem harder to see. Malaysia might win medals on home soil and declare that the worst is over.
But the real test will be whether the athletes who emerge in Kuala Lumpur have a pathway beyond the Games.
That is what Boonson and Pereira represent — continuity.

Pereira's success has been built around an athlete and coach who have worked together for years. Boonson's performances show what can happen when youthful talent continues to move forward instead of merely being celebrated for its potential. Malaysia needs that progression.
Perhaps that explains why Malaysians found themselves cheering for Boonson and Pereira.
Fans do not owe a flag their admiration. They give it to excellence when they see it.
Boonson made the track feel fast. Pereira made it feel dramatic. They gave spectators something to believe in.
Malaysian athletics needs to give Malaysians that feeling again.
Not through slogans. Not through another restructuring exercise. Not by promising that the next Games will be different.
But by building athletes who can walk onto an Asian track and look as though they belong there.
There is less than a year before the SEA Games come to Kuala Lumpur.
That is not enough time to repair everything. It is enough time to decide whether Nagoya was a warning or merely another result.
The first step is not winning a medal — it is admitting there is a problem.

5b1fa80e5759bf96: Sultan Perak, Sultan Nazrin Shah secara agak mendadak dan tiba-tiba menzahirkan dukacita mendalam baginda terhadap budaya perbincangan dan perdebatan, yang menurutnya sudah menjauhi muafakat, tetapi mengarah kepada pertelagahan tanpa adab. Amatlah penting bagi bangsa kita dan umat Islam, dididik membudayakan sikap mendengar sebelum menjawab, memahami sebelum menghukum dan meneliti sebelum menyebarkan sesuatu.”

Kebimbangan Sultan Nazrin itu ternyata mendalam kerana Baginda turut mengingatkan masyarakat supaya 'tidak menjadi insan yang hanya mahu didengar tetapi tidak mahu mendengar, mudah menghukum tetapi enggan memahami atau berbicara mengenai perpaduan sedangkan kata-kata sendiri menyalakan perpecahan'.

Sebenarnya, fenomena cita bencana yang disebut-sebut oleh Sultan Nazrin itu boleh dikesani paling banyak tumbuh melalang di pelbagai platform media sosial. Masing-masing mengulas, mengomentar, menulis pandangan tanpa tapis, tanpa berfikir dan tidak mengingat dosa.

Dalam krisis yang menimpa Negeri Sembilan, kini telah berlarutan hampir enam bulan; fitnah mengenai tanah adat, waris-waris bertikai, dan aneka macam lagi, tampak menjadi-jadi. Media menggunakan istilah kemelut untuk menggambarkan konflik gila ini. Tetapi, sebenarnya tiada kemelut. Yang ada hanyalah 'ke-mulut'. Atau, kemulut.

Mengapakah ia bukan kemelut? Tetapi kemulut? Apakah kemelut dan apakah kemulut? Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka menghurai kemelut sebagai keadaan atau saat genting lagi berbahaya dan ia adalah berkenaan ekonomi, atau politik, di mana ia ditanggapi semacam satu kegen­tingan, krisis, atau dalam erti kata lain kebalikan kepada kestabilan dan keharmonian.

Kemulut adalah satu istilah ciptaan sendiri untuk memaparkan secara palsu satu-satu keadaan atau saat itu sebagai genting lagi berbahaya demi agenda atau objektif politik tertentu yang biasanya adalah untuk beroleh kuasa, keuntungan bisnes, projek, atau melepaskan diri dari satu-satu hukuman jenayah seperti contohnya rasuah, dan korupsi. Kemulut dinamai kemulut kerana mereka yang bekerja untuk memalsukan keadaan ini akan beroleh upah berbayar, wang habuan, gaji hadiah supaya kegentingan berterusan sehinggalah kelak padam sendiri lantaran basi atau dalam bahasa Inggeris, overtaken by events.

Gejala kemulut ini sangat berkait rapat dengan gerakan politik lasykar siber satu terma atau istilah digunakan untuk menjelaskan perihal aktivis parti politik yang diupah untuk membenih, menyebar dan menggandakan kesan propaganda politik di media. Kepesatan media sosial menjadikan mereka ini dikesani dengan mudah di Facebook, TikTok atau X. Fenomena kemulut lasykar siber ini mula dikesani dengan ketara ketika kempen PRU-12 dan meledak menjelang pilihan raya ke-14, dan ke-15. Ia semakin menjadi-jadi sekarang memandangkan suhu politik di negara kita kian menaik ekoran siri pilihan raya di Johor, Negeri Sembilan dan Melaka tidak lama lagi.

Gerakan lasykar siber tidak sama dengan kekecohan para warganet atau jaguh siber. Kedua-dua gelar ini, warganet dan juara siber biasanya adalah organik dan merupakan reaksi spontan tanpa terstruktur. Namun, keberadaan warganet dan jaguh siber ini sangat rapat dengan lasykar siber. Sebagai satu bandingan, lasykar siber menanam benih atau naratif politik tertentu, dan mereka itu berbayar, dan apabila sesuatu isu menjadi genting dan kemelut, warganet dan jaguh siber yang terdiri dari pengguna media sosial orang awam akan memberi reaksi segera atau spontan. Warganet dan jaguh siber ini tidak dibayar, dan kadangkala memberi respons biadab, antiadab, menyala-nyalakan pergaduhan dan seperti digambarkan oleh baginda Sultan Perak sebagai degil dan hanya mahu didengar tetapi enggan mendengar, cepat melompat menghukum seraya sengaja menolak untuk memahami sesuatu isu itu. Kebiasaannya tukang bakar iaitu lasykar siber ini akan terus mengapi-apikan keadaan dengan menjadikan nafsu ketaasuban sebagai kayu bakar.
Warganet dan jaguh siber yang tidak tahu dalang di sebalik kemulut itu akan terus menari mengikut rentak mereka.

Fenomena kemulut ini dalam ilmu sains politik adalah apa yang dinamakan sebagai political astroturfing. Para kemulut ini tahu bila perlu bertindak, dan mempunyai mekanisme tindak balas yang teratur untuk mengurang atau menggandakan impak kegiatan mereka. Rauchfleisch Kovic, dalam penerbitan ilmiah bertajuk 'Digital astroturfing in politics: Definition, typology and countermeasures' pada 2018 dan terbit di jurnal bernama Studies in Communication Sciences, menyatakan political astroturfing ini ialah satu kaedah atau gerakan, kempen atau aktiviti politik dalam talian yang ditonjolkan sebagai sekadar aktiviti individu biasa atau orang awam, tetapi sebenarnya mereka adalah aktor politik berbayar (justeru kemulut) dan terdapat tuan atau majikan politik yang menggunakan khidmat mereka untuk terus-terusan menggerakkan aktiviti sebegini.

Political astroturfing, bukan gerakan atau sentimen akar umbi yang tulen tetapi ia ditampil sedemikian. Dalam banyak keadaan ia adalah kegiatan terancang dan diatur secara terpusat dari atas ke bawah. Political astroturfing juga adalah siri kempen maklumat palsu yang telah diprogramkan secara berpusat menerusi penyamaran identiti. Ia berlaku dengan pesat dalam talian dengan agenda mewujudkan satu bentuk penyelewengan maklumat bertujuan untuk mencipta tanggapan palsu bahawa sikap atau pandangan yang dilontar mereka itu mendapat sokongan meluas dalam masyarakat.

Kesimpulannya, political astroturfing adalah taktik aktor politik untuk mengelirukan masyarakat dengan informasi palsu, dengan menggunakan identiti atau profil palsu dengan maksud untuk memperdayakan masyarakat.

Astroturfing ini sudah tentu tidak mementingkan adab. Ia mementingkan mulut, dan perut; wang atau habuan, upah atau janji majikannya; di mana selalu bos mereka adalah parti atau tokoh politik. Justeru astroturfing ini berkait rapat dengan lasykar siber, yang bekerja mencipta kemelut untuk beroleh sesuatu ke mulut mereka. Warganet dan jaguh siber pula adalah mereka yang ditenggek.

Astroturfing, bukanlah political bots yang mana ia merujuk secara ringkasnya perkongsian konten media sosial dengan masyarakat secara khusus mengenai isu politik. Political bots ini tidak semestinya berniat jahat dan berkongsi maklumat palsu. Terdapat dalam kalangan mereka memang menumpukan masa terluang untuk berkongsi maklumat politik yang sahih, benar dan relevan, dan selalunya mereka tiada kesetiaan kepada sesuatu isu atau bos tertentu. Mereka secara jujur menggunakan medium media sosial sebagai suara politik mereka. Kejujuran mereka dapat dikenal pasti memandangkan kelompok ini tidak menggunakan akaun palsu, sebaliknya mempunyai akaun atau profil yang sah.

Ada kemungkinan besar kemelut di Negeri Sembilan misalnya digerakkan oleh kemulut sesetengah pihak yang berkepentingan. Mungkin, kemulut yang bertanggungjawab menciptakan kemelut di Negeri Sembilan itu beroleh kelulut lazat. Mungkin, tumpuan awal mereka adalah untuk mencipta ketidakstabilan politik di negeri tersebut dengan maksud untuk berlaku pilihan raya awal. Tujuan pilihan raya awal ini katakan, adalah untuk membolot kekayaan dan hasil mahsul negeri khusus dalam bentuk nadir bumi. Mudah-mudah orang awam, atau warganet biasa yang jahil pun terpedaya dan tertipu oleh kemulut ini.

1999d70e31b9acfb: Malaysia’s foreign minister Mohamad Hasan has raised one of the oldest and most uncomfortable questions surrounding the United Nations: why should five countries possess the power to prevent the UN Security Council from acting?
His argument that the veto should be challenged and ultimately abolished deserves serious attention. Expanding the Security Council alone cannot resolve its structural weaknesses.

More countries sitting around the table will mean little if five permanent members — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — continue to hold powers unavailable to everyone else.
Yet there is an enormous difference between recognising the problem and solving it.
Abolishing the veto is practical as an aspiration but almost impossible under the present international system.
The reason is straightforward.
The veto was not accidentally inserted into the UN Charter.
It was part of the political bargain underpinning the creation of the United Nations after the Second World War.
The major powers would participate in the new organisation so long as they could prevent decisions on substantive Security Council matters that fundamentally contradicted their interests.
That arrangement remains deeply entrenched.
Indeed, changing the UN Charter requires ratification by two-thirds of UN members, including all five permanent Security Council members.
The paradox could hardly be clearer: the countries that possess the veto effectively possess a veto over abolishing their own veto.
Why would they voluntarily surrender it?
Washington regards permanent membership and the veto as important instruments of American influence. Beijing and Moscow view theirs similarly.
London and Paris are unlikely to surrender one of the principal institutional privileges maintaining their status as permanent Security Council powers.
Great powers rarely relinquish entrenched advantages merely because others regard them as unfair.
Nevertheless, Mohamad is correct to challenge the principle.
The world of 2026 bears little resemblance to that of 1945.
India is among the world’s most important powers. Africa, despite having more than 50 UN members, lacks permanent representation.
Neither Latin America nor Southeast Asia possesses a permanent seat.
The Security Council therefore continues to carry the institutional DNA of the immediate postwar order.
Expanding its membership would improve representation.
But expansion without addressing the veto could merely create a larger council while preserving its fundamental inequality.
This is where Malaysia and other middle powers should concentrate their diplomatic efforts.
If immediate abolition is virtually impossible, constraining the political use of the veto is not.
The UN General Assembly has already established a mechanism requiring scrutiny when a permanent Security Council member exercises its veto.
Such mechanisms should be strengthened, particularly when the council is considering genocide, crimes against humanity or other grave violations of international humanitarian law.
Every veto should carry a political cost.
The permanent member using it should have to explain publicly why preventing collective action serves international peace and security.
The General Assembly should become increasingly assertive whenever the Security Council becomes paralysed.
For Asean, there is an important lesson here.
Southeast Asian countries cannot compete militarily with the major powers.
Asean’s influence has instead depended on consultation, institutional persistence, consensus and moral suasion.
Small and middle powers survive in an unequal international system not by pretending that power does not exist, but by creating rules and expectations that constrain how power is exercised.
The same principle should apply to the United Nations.
There is also a warning for the permanent five themselves.
The veto protects their national interests, but excessive reliance on it can progressively weaken the institution from which their privileged status derives.
If the Security Council repeatedly becomes incapable of acting precisely when international peace is most endangered, countries will increasingly seek other coalitions, institutions and arrangements.
The veto can therefore protect power while simultaneously eroding legitimacy.
Malaysia should consequently continue challenging it, even while recognising that formal abolition remains extraordinarily difficult.
International norms rarely disappear overnight. They weaken when practices once considered unquestionable become progressively harder to justify.
The veto emerged from the geopolitical realities of 1945. Eight decades later, the international community has every right to question whether those privileges should remain permanent.
Removing them presently may be close to impossible.
But allowing entrenched privilege to remain permanently beyond challenge would be worse.
It would leave the United Nations not merely constrained by great-power politics but increasingly imprisoned by it.
Asean has to keep expressing its opposition to a permanent system of great power privilege without end though.

fd382010ba317855: In 1947, a young Malay woman entered medical school in Singapore; she was the only Malay woman in her intake. I wonder what it felt like to walk into that classroom each morning, knowing there was nobody quite like you there.

Dr Hasmah Ali, also known as Siti Hasmah, went on to graduate, practise medicine and lead public health services. With her passing at the age of 100, we have lost someone who helped change what a doctor could look like in Malaysia.

Many knew her as the wife of a prime minister. She was that, and carried the role for decades, but she was a doctor before she was a public figure, and her medical work deserves to be remembered on its own terms.

After graduating in 1955, she worked in a hospital before devoting herself to maternal and child health in Kedah. In 1965, she became the first woman to be appointed as a medical officer in the maternal and child health department; in 1974, she became the state’s first female maternal and child health officer. She also led the rural health training school in Jitra.
Those appointments gave her responsibility for people’s care and for the health workers who would provide it.
Her teams travelled to villages to provide immunisation and health education. They worked with traditional midwives and spoke with families about pregnancy, childbirth and caring for newborns.

Hasmah understood that a mother could not always arrange transport, leave her responsibilities and appear at a clinic simply because a doctor wanted her there. Healthcare had to make the journey towards her.

I find that part of her story especially moving. It is easy to praise a pioneer for being a trailblazer. It takes longer to understand the patient work that followed: returning to communities, earning trust and teaching others to care for mothers and children.
She helped build a health service in which a woman’s judgment could guide that work.

The norm she challenged has changed profoundly for Malaysian women who came after her such as Dr Narimah Awin, who went on to lead family health services and advise the World Health Organization on maternal and reproductive health; Dr Adeeba Kamarulzaman, whose work on HIV took her into global leadership; and Dr Jemilah Mahmood, who founded Mercy Malaysia and now leads work in planetary health.

And of course, Dr Wan Azizah Wan Ismail, who took her experience as a doctor into national political life while continuing to support programmes and changes within the health landscape. Most recently, Dr BP Nirmala, a Malaysian cancer epidemiologist, joined the World Health Organization (WHO) science council this year.

For me, this is also personal. Dr S Saunthari leads the National Cancer Society of Malaysia, of which I now serve as a director. She is also the first Malaysian president-elect of the global NCD Alliance.

Around these well-known names are many more women leading wards, district services, classrooms and research teams. Each has earned their place. Together, they show how far women’s authority in medicine now reaches.
Hasmah lived another side of medicine when she was treated for breast cancer. In 2019, she spoke publicly about that experience.

The doctor who had spent years urging women to care for their health let us hear from her as a patient. Her illness did not define her life, but her willingness to speak about it was another way of making women’s health visible.

We should be careful not to assume that there is a straight line from one woman to the next. Hasmah did not create every opportunity that followed, and the women who came after her built their own careers.

But the legacy of her achievement was to help change expectations of them. She showed Malaysians a Malay woman practising medicine, teaching health workers and leading a service at a time when that was a rare sight.

She remains an icon because her example still asks something of us. When a young woman finds herself the only one in the room, will we recognise her ability and make room for her to lead? When a patient cannot reach care, will we go closer to them?
Hasmah answered those questions with her life. Her light continues in the women who enter medicine, in those who lead it, and in the people whose lives they change.

And as much as we will remember the former prime minister’s wife, we will also remember the doctor who went to mothers in the villages of Kedah, the teacher who prepared others to care for them, and the woman who spoke openly when she herself faced cancer.
Hasmah was always her own woman. Her work lives on in the people it reached; her example lives on in the women who follow. And she will remain, very dearly, in our hearts.

2ef764de3e420a81: About 66 million years ago, the Chicxulub asteroid smashed into Earth, kicking up tsunamis and dropping hot debris that annihilated non-avian dinosaurs and many other species. But not everything it left in its wake was destructive. This space rock hit what is now the partially submerged Yucatan Peninsula, and at the bottom of the ocean, the impact generated enough heat to create a hydrothermal system that persisted for 8 million years and may have been a hotbed of life.

When researchers drilled for samples in the impact zone in 2016, they studied the types of rock that had formed as a result of the asteroid strike. This gave more insight into what happened in the immediate and long-term aftermath of this cataclysmic event.

The collision was intense enough to cause deformation far beneath the surface. Subterranean effects reached 35 km (almost 22 miles) down, and included the melting an immense amount of rock. Exposure to seawater made that rock porous. As hot water seeped into the pores, a hydrothermal system formed. The hot water gushing into an isolated region of the freezing depths could have attracted microorganisms and possibly other life forms that were otherwise struggling to survive.

693af3d566f66457: OpenAI, which hoovered up vast amounts of internet content amid copyright fights, has accused individuals associated with China’s Moonshot AI of being involved in a "distillation attack" that began July 1. The house of Altman warns that extracting its models’ reasoning at scale could help rivals train capable models without preserving the same guardrails. Model distillation is a machine learning technique that can involve using one model’s outputs to train another – in adversarial cases, by sending bulk queries designed to reproduce the larger model’s reasoning and capabilities. Both the feds and major US AI companies, including Google and Anthropic, have accused Chinese rivals - and specifically Moonshot AI - of using distillation to reproduce capabilities from American models. In a Wednesday blog, OpenAI chimed in, saying it spotted and ultimately disrupted an adversarial distillation campaign that ran nearly all of July. “The operators did not break our encryption, compromise a database, or gain direct access to stored user conversations,” according to the blog. “Instead, they manipulated model interactions so that protected reasoning could be reproduced in forms visible to the requester in a coordinated, scaled manner that violated our terms of service.” The queries began on July 1, and while they started slowly, “we observed high-volume spikes on July 24 and 25 consisting of 16,000 requests using a relevant extraction pattern from over 4,000 users,” OpenAI said. Upon investigating the incident, the AI giant identified related “prompt-pattern activity” across more than 15,000 users. OpenAI fully disrupted the campaign on July 28, we’re told. While OpenAI said that it's unclear whether all of the operators during the July time period were linked to just one rival AI company, the “core cluster” of the theft came from Moonshot AI, which developed Kimi. The Register reached out to Moonshot AI for comment and did not receive an immediate response. We also asked OpenAI which of its models were targeted during the July campaign, but did not hear back. It’s worth noting that, in late July, US President Donald Trump’s Assistant for Science and Technology Michael Kratsios also accused Moonshot AI of creating its Kimi K3 model by distilling Anthropic’s Fable. Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 model, released a week ago, comes with a defense against distillation called "preserved thinking" that it introduced with Fable 5.1. “Adversarial distillation poses safety and national security risks,” OpenAI said on Wednesday, echoing earlier gripes from American companies and government officials. “Extracted reasoning could be used to train another model without preserving the safeguards applied to the original model’s user-facing outputs,” OpenAI added. “At scale, distillation can also accelerate the transfer of advanced capabilities without requiring the same investment in safety. These concerns become heightened as models gain capabilities in dual use domains.” In response, OpenAI said it banned the model-copying accounts tightened signup and infrastructure controls and expanded monitoring efforts. It also “closed a pathway that allowed someone who already possessed another user's encrypted reasoning to replay it and recover its contents,” and worked with service providers to ensure that this type of distillation activity didn’t just move to third-party services. Additionally, OpenAI shared the details of its investigation with other AI firms, through the Frontier Model Forum, and government information-sharing programs.®

4530dbe65ddfbc46: Mechanical calculators are precise, fascinating gadgets that you wouldn’t think would take well to being 3D printed, but a YouTuber has proved that a pocket-sized unit can be made purely from plastic filament. YouTuber 3D all Workshop detailed his working, but limited, build in a recent video. If you’re familiar with the holy grail of palm-sized mechanical calculators, the Curta, also known as the “pepper mill,” you already have a working understanding of how this 3D-printed calculator works. As detailed in the video, Workshop’s 3D-printed mechanical calculator, like the Curta, relies on a more than 200-year-old component known as the Leibniz stepped drum, named for its inventor, German philosopher and mathematician Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. The core concept of the calculator’s central mechanism, like that of many other mechanical calculators, is the Leibniz drum’s teeth of different lengths. There are nine teeth per drum, representing values one through nine, while a zero setting engages none of them. Workshop’s 3D printed calculator can take inputs from 1 to 999, with one drum per digit. You use a lever to move a gear up the drum so that it only activates as many teeth as are needed for a particular number. The same concept is used to input values into the Curta, just in a much more precise manner - one of the big benefits of using machined aluminum over 3D printing filament. As a result of wanting to keep the 3D printed calc’s build palm-sized, the YouTuber was forced to restrict what it’s able to do. It can do addition, and the addition of a multi-wheel enables it to also do multiplication by simply performing multiple sequences of adding the same number. The Curta does multiplication in a similar manner, requiring a user to input their base number and the number of times they want to multiply by addition. Unlike the Curta, Workshop’s calculator can’t subtract, nor can it divide - as its creator explains, there simply wasn’t the room to get all those fiddly bits into a palm-sized device. It’s not clear how large it would have to be to add those functions, but if the 3x-sized 3D printed Curta is any indication - its creator said the increased size was necessary - it’d probably be quite large. Scaling down to Workshop’s tiny 3D printed calculator means plenty of issues were bound to arise, and they definitely did. “There were a lot of problems,” he noted, explaining that “even the tiniest inconsistencies when printing can cause problems.” If you’ve ever used a 3D filament printer, you know how often such inconsistencies pop up. Gears kept binding because of tight 3D-printing tolerances, while backlash (the play between mating mechanical parts) could throw the drums out of sync. Pieces kept breaking during redesigns, and even the vibrations from picking up and using the calculator were enough to disrupt its components. The YouTuber went through roughly 100 design iterations over the two-month project, finally addressing the problems with custom-designed 3D-printed springs and a ratchet mechanism that kept backlash from throwing the drums out of sync. All said, the final build ended up with 109 separate pieces, took 17 print-hours to complete, and used 90g of filament. Despite multiple calls on YouTube for 3D all Workshop to publish, or even sell, his design, he has yet to make it available, so no struggling through a day-long print job for a potentially brief moment playing with this one. In the meantime, you could 3D print the giant Curta, or if you have a couple grand lying around begging to be spent, try to get your hands on an original. ®

3e98ea49575d5b71: The Trump administration's export control policies governing the sale of AI accelerators to China haven't stopped homegrown Huawei from filling the void. In a Q&A-style release this week, the company's rotating chairman Eric Xu claimed that its Ascend line of neural processing units (NPUs) had exceeded Nvidia in Chinese market share. "It's pretty hard to collect data about the market share of Nvidia in China, but based on the data we have collected, Ascend has surpassed Nvidia," he said. "Chinese people have a keen sense of urgency, and will not accept a future in which others decide whether or not we can have access to certain products." Since taking office, the Trump administration has done an about-face on export controls. After imposing new licensing requirements on Nvidia's and AMD's China-spec accelerators in April 2025, the US Commerce Department reversed course that summer, later reaching an arrangement to cut the US government in on a percentage of certain China-bound chip sales. By late last year, the Trump administration loosened restrictions further, announcing that Nvidia would be allowed to sell its more potent H200-series parts to approved Chinese customers for the first time ever. However, the damage was already done. While Uncle Sam had given Jensen Huang its blessing to resume sales, the initial blockade of H20s earlier in the year had set off alarm bells in Beijing. Government officials there began pressuring bit barn operators to transition away from foreign accelerators in favor of homegrown alternatives. During Nvidia's Q2 earnings call, executives revealed that while the company had begun shipments of a small volume of H200 accelerators to the region, they amounted to less than 1 percent of its datacenter revenues. "Even though our chips may be less advanced, at least their supply is assured, so that you don't have to worry about chip supply day in and day out," Xu said. "For the Chinese government, for the domestic industry, and for Huawei, the path forward is undoubtedly to push for full self-sufficiency in terms of chips and the entire semiconductor value chain." As we recently discussed, while Huawei's latest accelerators still fall short of Nvidia's or AMD's on paper, they make up for that deficit with scale. Huawei is currently deploying a 256,000-card Atlas 950 SuperCluster, while its newer architecture is designed to support training and inference for multi-trillion-parameter models and scale to as many as one million NPUs. However, as Xu notes, Huawei likely won't be a threat to Nvidia outside of China for a while. "We don't have enough capacity to satisfy the demand in China. We don't have plans to expand the international market in a fully-fledged way," he said, downplaying reports that Huawei had begun supplying friendly nations with its chips. "The balance between satisfying the needs of domestic customers and those of international customers is actually quite easy," he said when asked about the use of Ascend accelerators to power Malaysia's sovereign AI initiative. "We prioritize Chinese customers who are in urgent demand for compute; outside of China we only supply a very limited number of customers who either have no access to alternative solutions or want an alternative solution." Along with pressure from government officials to transition away from foreign chips, changing software paradigms are making the transition easier for model devs, like DeepSeek, which has been working with Huawei's chips for well over a year now. "The first barrier encountered by Ascend is actually not hardware itself," said Liao Heng, chief scientist of Huawei's HiSilicon. "It's primarily the ecosystem barrier, because two years ago there was still a tremendous software barrier for Ascend." Liao is referring to what's often called the CUDA moat, a software hurdle not unique to China but faced by essentially every competing chipmaker. 0b8f0b7c11474e44: What comes next after a moment when companies sell existential risk but pursue public funding and DIY regulation, even as software developers question their life choices? Peter Norvig, distinguished education fellow at Stanford HAI and former Google research director, used his opening keynote at The AI Conference in San Francisco on Wednesday to speculate on the answer. Almost certainly, it's another AI conference – on Thursday in fact – given the two or three dozen of them that have bubbled up in San Francisco this year or are scheduled in the remaining three months. To get to the present, he took a detour through the past. He acknowledged the milestones of AlexNet and ImageNet in 2012, the Transformer architecture for machine learning in 2017, the debut of ChatGPT in 2022, and the emergence of reasoning and coding agents in 2024. He also touched on the sudden competency of AI models for math, noting that two years ago, GPT-4 couldn't count the number of "r"s in "strawberry." Yet as of August this year, he observed, 25 percent of math preprint papers on arXiv acknowledged AI assistance. Norvig went on to cite Linux kernel creator Linus Torvalds' changing attitude toward AI. "Six months ago he was a skeptic, he became a cautious adopter, and now he's a dogmatic advocate," said Norvig. So what now? Norvig says the process of software engineering needs to change. The tech industry has changed many times before, he said, pointing to transitions from plugging wires into mainframes, to assembly language, to higher level programming languages. "At every step you have to change the way you think about what software engineering is," he said. And now we're going to have to change it all again. How do we do specifications and documentation? How do we capture this theory of the evolving program that we're not capturing well now?" To illustrate that point, Norvig recounted some of his recent work. "I did an embarrassing thing the other day, right? So I'm using Codex, [and I] write some stuff that seems to work," he said. He told Codex to send the pull request for review, and his colleague asked why he was checking in 6,000 temp files. "And I said, 'Well, I didn't notice that,'" Norvig explained. "And sure enough, I had written 6,000 temporary files, and Codex thought that it wanted to check those in. So I told [Codex], 'No, don't check them in, just delete them.' At first I thought, shame on me. I should have looked before I asked for a code review on that. And I just skipped that step of looking. Maybe I should be doing that." Then, said Norvig, he thought that the GPT model should have known that he didn't want to save 6,000 temporary files, so as not to burden the reviewer. And then he mused that if you have enough storage and memory, maybe it would be useful to have those files to have a more thorough history of how the codebase changed. "So the expectations of what's good practice and how that's going to change, that's all going to be different," he said. And that's just the start. "We gotta get the security and privacy and data pipelines and supply chains, those are all gonna be different in how they interact with each other," he said. "This idea of continuous integration and recursive self-improvement. How much do we let the systems go off on their own and how are we monitoring them?" Judging by the steady drip of incidents where AI models have hacked into third-party websites, discovered only after someone scrutinized log files, we're not monitoring them. So yeah, there's work to be done. ®

7abe4fd20663f058: A 16-year-old security researcher named Faav found an authentication flaw in Microsoft’s Titan analytics service that allowed him to gain administrator access, submit unauthorized SQL queries with no valid credentials, and potentially reach analytics databases containing an estimated 17.3 trillion stored rows. Titan is an internal analytics platform, and Redmond restricts access via its web interface to Microsoft employees. Faav, with an assist from an AI hackbot he built called Antares, found that he could access Titan’s API through an Azure Cloud Services host because Titan didn’t check the signature on a login token. Microsoft has since locked down the API and paid Faav a $5,000 bug bounty for his research. He says the breakthrough came after 10 days of authentication errors, when he returned to the problem after finishing Friday’s schoolwork and finally managed to execute SQL as a Titan admin after 1 AM Saturday. “It was 2 AM,” Faav said in a blog about his findings. “I wanted to yell, or at least say something out loud, but my parents were asleep. So I just sat there staring at 17,333,335,124,315 and checked the math again.” He also notes that he rewrote his blog post at Microsoft’s request, cut sections and numbers, and reworded the impact prior to publication. “We appreciate the opportunity to investigate the findings reported by Faav,” Microsoft said in a statement provided to Faav for his blog. “Their submission and coordinated vulnerability disclosure helped us to better protect our customers by hardening our services. We value and appreciate safe security research under the terms of the Microsoft Bug Bounty Program and look forward to continuing to work with Faav in the future.” A boy and his bot The research began on August 25 when Antares found Titan’s public API. For the next 10 days, the human and bot tested the service’s JSON Web Token (JWT) authentication checks and email-formatted user principal names (UPNs), eventually finding an unsigned token that could reach Titan’s local user lookup - but not a UPN that Titan recognized. Early on September 5, Faav changed the unsigned token’s UPN from an email-formatted identity to admin. Titan recognized it as a local username, resolved it to local user ID 1, which held an admin role, and allowed him to run SQL. The takeaway, according to Faav: Titan validated the contents of the JWT (tenant, audience, app ID, user) but never verified the signature, the most important part of any authentication check. The authentication checks felt like a hotel where every door had a working keycard reader, but any keycard unlocked any room. Despite all the access-control logic existing in the app, the one missing piece made it all pointless. If you’re a developer (or coding agent) reading this, the most important takeaway from this post is to make sure you verify signatures above all else when building auth. This gave Faav access to Titan’s platform metadata database, and from there he could query application tables directly. The metadata contained: About 25,000 account and email records. 17,990 employee email records. 15,001 employee organization records. 355 database configurations. 20,979 virtual-dataset SQL definitions. 24,569 dashboards, 425,891 charts, and 27,347 dataset definitions. Titan’s user and usage directory exposed employee job titles, departments, and management hierarchy, which the researcher notes could be useful for social-engineering attacks - “though I never tested or demonstrated that,” he added. He also found a Bing analytics sample and tested two rows that contained search info, identifiers, and high-level location information, such as country- or state-level details. Faav said the location values did not contain precise user locations. 17.3 trillion data rows Then he hit the jackpot, testing 56 routing values from an archived configuration and discovering 30 were still active. “Each routing value pointed to a backend configuration, and each configuration contained one or more databases, so the 30 live values resolved through 24 configurations to 17 connected analytics databases spanning 9,863 unique table names,” the bug hunter wrote. The total comes to about 17.3 trillion rows, which Faav says is a storage estimate derived from metadata and likely includes historical, duplicated, and derived data. “But quite the high number nonetheless.” Between September 6 and September 8, Microsoft asked the teen to stop testing and requested his IP address to confirm no nefarious activity beyond the bug bounty research. A day later, Redmond locked down the endpoint and told Faav the “report prompted immediate investigation and remediation to address the remaining exposure.” Microsoft awarded the bug hunter $5,000 for his work on September 17.®

73004a7fabbbd090: Resolute Raccoon is ready to roll out to existing Ubuntu users. Canonical has flipped the switch, and users on 24.04 will start to get offered 26.04.1. Canonical has marked the occasion with an official announcement that it's time to upgrade your desktop. Normally, a given LTS release of Ubuntu starts nagging offering the upgrade to the new release when the following LTS version gets its first point-release. This time around, there has been a substantial delay: Ubuntu 26.04.1 appeared over a month ago. The company announced a small delay in a post ubuntu-announce mailing list when 26.04.1 first appeared, saying: “Users of Ubuntu 24.04 LTS will be offered an automatic upgrade to 26.04.1 LTS via Update Manager a couple of weeks following this release after some planned backports to address regressions in a recent version of rust-coreutils.” The delay is the fault of Rust language which is aiming to replace C, as promoted by evangelistic developers whom Linux grandees castigate until they go away. This is the same Rust uutils bundle that David Uhden Collado recently ported to OpenBSD, but which was swiftly rejected by determined defender of the C faith Theo de Raadt. (Please read the previous two paragraphs in the most sarcastic tone that you can muster.) If you want to upgrade your Ubuntu box, there are two potential methods – one command-line-based, and one using the GUI – but both are easier than the traditional Debian method. First, though, install any and all outstanding updates. For this, we entering the following the shell command, if only because it’s easier to copy-and-paste: sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y ; sudo snap refresh Because Canonical uses phased updates, you may see that some updates are “held back”. If you do, you can just run the main command again to get them: sudo apt full-upgrade -y Second time around, it may install a few more. Then reboot, and with any luck you will get offered the Resolute Raccoon upgrade. If you have Ubuntu installed on a relatively small partition, it may be as well to clear the APT package manager’s cache before you start. This can free up a lot of room. On our test VM, where we do this regularly, we got 1 GB back: liam-proven@noble-vbox:~$ df -h / Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on /dev/sda2 24G 18G 4.3G 81% / liam-proven@noble-vbox:~$ sudo apt clean liam-proven@noble-vbox:~$ df -h / Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on /dev/sda2 24G 17G 5.9G 74% / We reckon a free gigabyte for one command is pretty good. If you don’t get offered the upgrade automatically, run the “Software Updater” tool. If you don’t see it in your preferred app launcher, you can run the update-manager command in a shell. If you have any outstanding updates to your current version, you will be offered them first. Once they are all done, you should see a message saying: “The software on this computer is up-to-date. “However, Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS is now available (you have 24.04).” Alternatively, if you prefer to do these things from the shell: liam-proven@noble-vbox:~$ do-release-upgrade Checking for a new Ubuntu release = Welcome to Ubuntu 26.04 LTS 'Resolute Raccoon' = The Ubuntu team is proud to announce Ubuntu 26.04 LTS 'Resolute Raccoon'. We’ve cut this to the first few lines – there are some 60 lines of it in full. As we reported when it came out, there are worthwhile novelties in RR. For instance, in our testing on some machines with older Nvidia GPUs which did not work well with 24.04, the now Wayland-only GNOME 50 drove our geriatric video cards just fine. If you use any other desktop, from Cinnamon to Unity, you still get X11. ®

748de2112c17524e: According to the US President, the term Artificial Intelligence (AI) is tired while "Super Intelligence" is wired. Trump has issued an executive order to compel the Federal Government to use the new name instead. The term Artificial Intelligence was introduced by American computer and cognitive scientist John McCarthy in 1956, although the concept derives at least in part from work by British mathematician Alan Turing published in 1950. Regardless of its origin, the technology has outgrown the term, and the US, in particular, should adopt a new one, according to the man in the Oval Office. “The capabilities of today’s frontier systems do much more than imitate or automate discrete aspects of human intelligence. They increasingly amplify human ingenuity and unlock new forms of creativity, empowering Americans to achieve what was previously impossible across science, medicine, and nearly every other domain of human endeavor," he said in an executive order, which has the power to direct Federal agencies' behavior. "As these capabilities continue to improve, they increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence, but a new era of Super Intelligence,” he added. Accordingly, the order directs federal government to “reflect the transformative capabilities of these technologies and the limitless opportunities they create for the American people”. Trump said that because “Super Intelligence” is more apt for “advancing capabilities of these technologies”, the executive branch should use the terms “Super Intelligence” and “SI” in place of “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI”. The order says the executive branch “will not acknowledge the usage of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI' in any applicable setting”. The president also orders that government websites, official correspondence, public communications and policy documents reflect this change. The question is why the sudden change? It orders the “upgrading of American systems for advanced AI” and promises Federal Government access to “frontier models”. We’re guessing all that paperwork will now have to be pulped. Others are speculating about motives aside from any sudden leap forward in technology over the last three months or so. Posting on X, Adam Cochran, a managing partner at Canadian VC firm Cinneamhain Ventures, claimed the decision to publish the executive order could be linked to investments in the .si domains over the last three months, which he argued would rise in popularity among governments and companies wishing to curry favor with the US administration. Although unable to produce categorical evidence that these investments could be linked to the President, his family or business associates, Cochran pointed toward a spike in domain registrations with the suffix .si, including 12,000 MAGA-related domains. In the few months leading up to the announcement, people also registered more than 10,000 AI-related terms to the .si domains, he claimed, some of which, he added, have now been relisted for millions of dollars. In the absence of any overriding evidence, a right-thinking person is forced to weigh the most likely explanation, balancing the probability that the US has entered the era of super intelligence and must change its paperwork and website registration accordingly to maintain its technological superiority, against the chance that the executive order is part of a shameless domain-name grift. ®
